questions.q: Why is `np.linalg.solve(A, b)` preferred over computing `np.linalg.inv(A) @ b`?
options: inv(A) @ b produces a completely different mathematical answer
solve is both faster and more numerically stable, since computing an explicit inverse does unnecessary extra work that amplifies rounding error
np.linalg.inv does not exist in current NumPy versions
solve only works when A is symmetric
questions.explain: Both approaches solve the same mathematical problem, but computing an explicit matrix inverse introduces unnecessary computation and amplifies floating-point rounding error compared to solving the system directly.

questions.q: Why should you use `np.linalg.eigh` rather than the general `np.linalg.eig` for a covariance matrix?
options: eigh only works on matrices with negative eigenvalues
Covariance matrices are symmetric, and eigh exploits that structure to be faster and numerically more reliable than the general-purpose eig
eig cannot be used on any matrix larger than 2x2
eigh and eig always return different, unrelated results
questions.explain: Covariance matrices are square and symmetric, guaranteeing real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. eigh is specialized for this case and is both faster and more numerically reliable than the fully general eig.

questions.q: How does SVD on a mean-centered data matrix relate to PCA?
options: They are unrelated techniques that happen to share the word 'component'

The right singular vectors of the centered data matrix are the principal component directions, and this path is generally more numerically stable than forming the covariance matrix and eigendecomposing it
SVD can only be used on square matrices, so it cannot be applied to a data matrix
PCA requires computing the matrix inverse first, which SVD does not support
questions.explain: For a centered data matrix, the right singular vectors from SVD correspond directly to PCA's principal component directions, and computing PCA this way avoids the extra rounding error introduced by explicitly forming X^T X.

questions.q: What does a very large condition number for a matrix indicate?
options: The matrix has unusually large numeric values that need to be rescaled
The matrix is well-conditioned and safe to invert directly
The system is highly sensitive to small input errors (including ordinary floating-point rounding), such as occurs with a near-singular, highly correlated covariance matrix
The matrix cannot be used with np.linalg.solve at all
questions.explain: A large condition number means small perturbations in the input (including floating-point rounding error) can be amplified into large errors in the solution — a common situation with near-singular covariance matrices from highly correlated assets.

questions.q: What is the practical relationship between a covariance matrix C, portfolio weights w, and portfolio variance?
options: Portfolio variance equals w^T C w, and the eigendecomposition of C reveals which directions in weight-space concentrate that risk
Portfolio variance is always equal to the largest single asset's variance
Covariance matrices cannot be used to compute portfolio variance; only correlation matrices can
Portfolio variance equals the determinant of C
questions.explain: Portfolio variance is the quadratic form w^T C w. Eigendecomposing C identifies the orthogonal directions (eigenvectors) along which risk is uncorrelated, each scaled by its own eigenvalue (variance).
